chapter_title: Understanding Variables: Storing Data in Blueprints
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the world of variables in Unreal Engine 5 Blueprints! Think of variables as named containers that hold pieces of information your game needs to remember and use. Just like in real life, you might need to keep track of a player's score, whether a door is open, or where an enemy should spawn. Variables are how Blueprints store all this dynamic data. Without them, your game would be static and unresponsive, unable to react to player input or changes in the game world.

Unreal Engine provides a rich set of variable types, each designed to hold a specific kind of data. The most common primitive types you'll encounter are:
*   **Boolean:** A simple true/false value. Perfect for states like `IsDoorOpen`, `HasKey`, or `IsPlayerAlive`.
*   **Integer:** A whole number (e.g., 0, 1, 100, -5). Useful for `PlayerScore`, `AmmoCount`, or `EnemyHealth`.
*   **Float:** A number with decimal points (e.g., 3.14, 0.5, 99.99). Ideal for `PlayerSpeed`, `DamageAmount`, or `TimeRemaining`.
*   **String:** A sequence of characters, essentially text (e.g., "Hello World", "Player Name"). Great for `DialogueText` or `ItemDescription`.

Beyond these primitives, Blueprints also offer more complex data structures essential for game development:
*   **Vector:** Represents a point in 3D space (X, Y, Z coordinates) or a direction. Critical for `PlayerLocation`, `SpawnPoint`, or `MovementDirection`.
*   **Rotator:** Represents a rotation in 3D space (Roll, Pitch, Yaw). Used for `CameraRotation` or `DoorOrientation`.
*   **Transform:** Combines a Vector (Location), a Rotator (Rotation), and a Vector (Scale) into a single structure. This is the complete representation of an object's position, orientation, and size in the world.
*   **Object Reference:** This is incredibly powerful. Instead of storing a value, an Object Reference stores a link to an actual Actor or Component in your game world. For example, you might have a variable `TargetDoor` of type `BP_Door_C` (a Blueprint class you've created) that allows your script to directly interact with a specific door in the level. This is how you make one Blueprint "talk" to another.

To create a variable in the Blueprint Editor, you'll navigate to the "My Blueprint" panel on the left side. Click the `+ Variable` button. You'll then name your variable (e.g., `PlayerHealth`) and select its type from the "Details" panel on the right. It's good practice to give variables clear, descriptive names using PascalCase (e.g., `IsPlayerDead`, `CurrentScore`). After creating a variable, remember to compile your Blueprint (the "Compile" button in the toolbar) so the changes are saved and recognized. In the "Details" panel, you can also set a default value for your variable, which is its initial state when the game starts or the Blueprint is spawned. For instance, `PlayerHealth` might default to `100.0`, and `IsDoorOpen` to `False`.

Variables also have a concept called **scope**. Most variables you create in the "My Blueprint" panel are **member variables**, meaning they belong to the entire Blueprint and can be accessed and modified by any event or function within that Blueprint. However, you can also create **local variables** within functions. These variables only exist and are accessible within that specific function, which helps keep your code organized and prevents unintended side effects. For beginners, focusing on member variables is a good starting point.

Once a variable is created, you'll interact with it in the Event Graph using **Get** and **Set** nodes. To get a variable's current value, simply drag the variable from the "My Blueprint" panel onto the Event Graph and select "Get [Variable Name]". To change its value, drag it onto the graph and select "Set [Variable Name]". The "Set" node requires an execution pin to trigger the change and an input pin for the new value. The "Get" node simply outputs the current value.

A common mistake beginners make is forgetting to compile their Blueprint after creating or modifying variables. If you try to use a new variable and it doesn't appear in the context menu, or your changes aren't taking effect, always check if your Blueprint needs compiling. Another frequent issue is type mismatch: trying to assign a Float value to an Integer variable, for example. Unreal Engine's Blueprint system is quite robust and will often prevent these errors with visual cues or compile warnings, but it's important to understand why they occur. Always ensure the data type you're providing matches the data type the variable expects. Mastering variables is the first step towards creating truly dynamic and interactive gameplay experiences.

screens.title: Understanding Variables: Storing Data in Blueprints
screens.subtitle: Why variables make gameplay dynamic, and how Blueprints store game state

narration.text: Variables are the memory of your Blueprint scripts. In gameplay you use variables to remember things that change: a player's score, whether a door is open, or an enemy's position. In Unreal Engine Blueprints, variables are named containers with a specific data type. That type controls what values the variable can hold, for example true/false for a Boolean or a three-component position for a Vector. Learning to create variables, choose appropriate types, set sensible defaults, and use Get and Set nodes is the first practical step toward scripting interactive behavior without writing C++. This chapter teaches you how to create primitive variables like Boolean, Integer, Float, and String, as well as complex types such as Vector, Rotator, Transform, and Object Reference. You will also learn scope differences between member and local variables and common troubleshooting steps like compiling and resolving type mismatches. By the end, you should be able to build a simple interactive actor that stores and updates state, and to reason about which type fits a given gameplay need. Think about one thing your game must remember — that is what a variable will store for you. How would you name it?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Variables let Blueprints retain and use changing game data by name and type, enabling interactive, dynamic behaviors.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Understanding Variables
Understanding Variables
Store game state with typed, named containers so your Blueprints can react to change.
Variables are the building blocks of interactive scripts. They give your Actor memory and let you read or change that memory at runtime with Get and Set nodes. Throughout this chapter you’ll see how to choose types, set defaults, manage scope, and avoid common mistakes like forgetting to compile or mismatching types.
In this lesson

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify when a variable is needed and select the right variable type for a gameplay purpose. You will create and name variables inside the Blueprint Editor, set sensible default values, and organize variables so your Blueprints remain understandable. You will also understand the difference between member variables, which belong to a Blueprint instance, and local variables, which live only inside a function. These objectives give you a practical skill set: pick a gameplay state to remember, create the variable, set a default, and change it in response to events. Practicing these steps builds confidence so you can script interactive gameplay without writing C++ code.

screens.title: What is a Variable in Blueprints?
screens.subtitle: Define variables and relate them to gameplay state

narration.text: A variable is a named container that holds a single piece of data for a Blueprint instance. That data can be simple, like true or false, or complex, like a three-component position. In gameplay, variables are the way your Blueprints remember state across events. For example, a Boolean named bIsOpen can store whether a door is currently open, and a Float called PlayerHealth can store health points that change when damage is taken. This is different from a temporary calculation: variables persist on the actor while it exists, so separate events can read and update the same value. A common beginner misconception is to treat functions like storage; remember that functions compute values when called, while variables store values between calls. Think about a checkpoint system: you might store the player's last safe location in a Vector variable so you can return them after a fall. Variables also let Blueprints interact: an Object Reference variable can link one actor to another so one Blueprint can change a property on the other. The practical insight is this: whenever multiple events, animations, or scripts need to agree about a single piece of information, use a variable. That clarity helps you design predictable, testable behavior. What single piece of state in your current project would you store in a variable right now?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A variable is a persistent, named container in a Blueprint that stores a value other parts of the Blueprint can read or change.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is a Variable?
Variable — named container
Persistent storage for a single piece of data a Blueprint needs to remember
Variables persist on an actor and let separate events share and update information. Use them when multiple events must access the same state, such as whether an object is unlocked or the player's score.
Example
bIsOpen = False initially; an Interact event sets bIsOpen to True to open the door.
Misconception
Don’t confuse functions with storage: functions compute when called; variables hold state between calls.
Why it matters
Variables make gameplay dynamic and allow different systems to coordinate by sharing named state instead of duplicating logic.
Analogy
Think of variables as labeled boxes
Each box holds one kind of thing. If it’s labeled PlayerScore and only holds whole numbers, storing a decimal will cause a mismatch — the type constrains what fits in the box.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Use variables whenever you need persistent, shared state across events; name and type them clearly to avoid confusion.

screens.title: Primitive Data Types
screens.subtitle: Booleans, Integers, Floats and Strings — when to use each

narration.text: Unreal Blueprints provide common primitive types that fit most simple gameplay needs. A Boolean holds true or false and is ideal for binary states such as IsDoorOpen or HasKey. An Integer stores whole numbers and suits counters like PlayerScore or AmmoCount. A Float stores decimals and is useful for continuous values like PlayerSpeed, DamageAmount, or TimeRemaining. Strings hold sequences of characters for text such as dialogue lines or item names. Choosing the right primitive matters because each type limits what you can store and which operations are safe. For example, adding 1 to an Integer increments a whole number, while adding 1.5 to a Float preserves fractional precision. A common mistake is using a String to store numbers; that forces conversions and makes numeric math awkward. Concrete examples help: track whether a door is open with a Boolean bIsOpen, keep PlayerScore as an Integer to avoid fractional scores, and use PlayerSpeed as a Float so you can apply smooth acceleration. In the Editor, pick the correct type in the Details panel for each variable. When in doubt, think about how you will use the value: if you need arithmetic with decimals, prefer Float; if you only need yes/no, choose Boolean. That small decision reduces later type mismatch issues and keeps your Event Graph tidy.

keyIdea.title: Primitive types
keyIdea.text: Choose Boolean for true/false, Integer for whole counts, Float for decimal values, and String for text to match how you plan to use the data.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Primitive Data Types
Primitive Types at a Glance
Pick the type that best matches how the data will be used in gameplay.
Boolean
True/False. Use for binary states like bIsOpen or HasKey.
Integer
Whole numbers for counts like PlayerScore or EnemyCount.
Float
Decimal numbers for speed, time, and fine-grained values like PlayerSpeed.
String
Text for names, dialogue, and descriptions—avoid using for numeric math.
Example Scenarios
Door state
bIsOpen: Boolean. Only needs true or false to control opening logic.
Score
PlayerScore: Integer. Whole numbers ensure simple counting and comparisons.
Speed
PlayerSpeed: Float. Fractions matter for smooth movement and physics.
Key Takeaway

Match type to use. Choosing the right primitive reduces conversion work and prevents logic errors.

screens.title: Complex Types: Vector, Rotator, Transform, Object Reference
screens.subtitle: When to use spatial and reference types

narration.text: Beyond primitives, Blueprints offer compound types that match game needs for space and relationships. A Vector stores three components—X, Y, Z—and represents either a position in 3D space or a direction. Use Vector for PlayerLocation, SpawnPoint, or MovementDirection. A Rotator stores rotational components—Roll, Pitch, Yaw—and is used for orientations such as CameraRotation or DoorOrientation. Transform bundles Location (Vector), Rotation (Rotator), and Scale (Vector) into one value that fully describes an object's placement in the world. Finally, an Object Reference stores a link to an Actor or Component instance, allowing one Blueprint to directly manipulate another; for example, a TargetDoor variable of type BP_Door_C lets you open or close a specific door by calling its functions or changing its properties. These types matter because they carry structured data you’ll pass between systems. A common novice mistake is trying to break a Transform into separate floats manually instead of using the structured Transform type; using the proper type keeps the Editor’s tools and functions compatible. When designing variables, prefer the highest-level type that expresses your intent: store a Transform when you need full spatial control, or an Object Reference when you need interaction with another actor instance. That preserves clarity and leverages Blueprint nodes built for those types.

keyIdea.title: Complex types
keyIdea.text: Use Vector/Rotator/Transform for spatial data and Object Reference to link one Blueprint to another actor instance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Complex Types
Spatial & Reference Types
Choose structured types that match the data you need to pass between systems.
Vector
Three floats for X, Y, Z. Represents position or direction, used for SpawnPoint or MovementDirection.
Rotator
Roll, Pitch, Yaw. Use for rotations like CameraRotation or DoorOrientation.
Transform
Location + Rotation + Scale. Use when you need the full spatial state of an object.
Object Reference
Stores a reference to an Actor or Component instance so you can call functions or change properties on that object.
Scenario
BP_InteractiveDoor
Use a Vector for a specific spawn offset, a Rotator for door orientation, and an Object Reference to link the door to the player or an unlockable item so the door can check the player's inventory.
Pro tip
Pro Tip

Prefer structured types like Transform when the Editor offers nodes tailored for them; it simplifies wiring and reduces conversion work.

screens.title: Creating Variables in the Blueprint Editor
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: add, name, type, compile

narration.text: Creating a variable in the Blueprint Editor is a short, repeatable process. Open your Blueprint and locate the My Blueprint panel. Click + Variable to add a new entry, then give it a clear name using PascalCase such as PlayerHealth or bIsOpen. With the variable selected, use the Details panel to click the variable type drop-down and choose the appropriate type: Boolean, Integer, Float, String, Vector, Rotator, Transform, or an Object Reference to a specific Blueprint class. After setting the type, enter a sensible default value in the Details panel—this is the value the variable starts with when the actor spawns. Finally, click Compile to save changes and let the Editor update context menus and graph options. A common pitfall is not compiling: if the variable doesn’t appear in the right-click or drag menus, compile first. Another small but powerful practice is to prefix Boolean names with b or use clear nouns for references; this improves readability. After you compile, try dragging the variable into the Event Graph and choose Get or Set to begin wiring behavior. Practice this sequence until it becomes second nature: Add → Name → Type → Default → Compile → Use.

keyIdea.title: Add variable steps
keyIdea.text: Add + name in My Blueprint, set type and default in Details, then compile so the variable is available to the graph.

screens.title: Default Values and Naming Conventions
screens.subtitle: Set sensible defaults and name variables for clarity

narration.text: Default values define the initial state of a variable when the Blueprint spawns or the game begins. Setting defaults avoids unpredictable behavior and gives your actors sensible starting conditions. For example, set PlayerHealth to 100.0, bIsOpen to False, and RequiredKeys to 1. When you define defaults, think about typical gameplay: do you want the door locked at spawn, should an enemy start alive, or does a timer begin at zero? Naming conventions also reduce mistakes: use PascalCase for names and prefix Booleans with b to distinguish them quickly. Object Reference variables benefit from descriptive names like TargetDoor or PlayerReference so their purpose is obvious when wiring nodes. A useful workflow is to name and default immediately after creating the variable. That makes your Event Graph easier to read and reduces the chance of using an uninitialized value. If you later change a default, remember to Save and Compile. Finally, consistent naming helps teammates understand your Blueprints. When you revisit a graph weeks later, clear names and defaults let you reason about behavior faster than deciphering ambiguous labels. Adopt a small naming standard early and stick with it.

keyIdea.title: Defaults & names
keyIdea.text: Set defaults at creation and use clear naming (PascalCase, b-prefix for Booleans) so graphs stay readable and predictable.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Defaults & Naming
Defaults set expected state
Sensible defaults prevent uninitialized behavior and speed testing.
Example defaults
PlayerHealth = 100.0, bIsOpen = False, RequiredKeys = 1, DoorOpenSpeed = 2.0
Naming conventions
PascalCase for variables. Prefix Booleans with b. Use descriptive names for references like TargetDoor or PlayerReference.
Why this matters
Testing and readability
Defaults let you run the level immediately without adding initialization events, and good names help collaborators and future you understand intent at a glance.
Key Takeaway

Set sensible defaults and follow a naming convention to reduce errors and speed up debugging and collaboration.

screens.title: Variable Scope: Member vs Local
screens.subtitle: Who can see a variable and for how long

narration.text: Variable scope defines where and how long a variable is accessible. Member variables, created in the My Blueprint panel, belong to the Blueprint instance and are accessible across the Event Graph, functions, and timelines within that Blueprint. They persist for the life of the actor instance. Local variables are created inside a function and exist only for that function call—this prevents unintended access and accidental side effects, and it keeps internal calculations encapsulated. Use member variables when multiple events or functions must share state, such as a door’s open state that several events may read or set. Use local variables inside a function for temporary calculations that should not affect the broader Blueprint state. A common beginner error is overusing member variables for every temporary value; that clutter can cause unexpected interactions and make the graph hard to maintain. Another mistake is trying to access a local variable from outside its function; the Editor will not expose it. When designing Blueprints, prefer member variables for long-lived state and local variables for short-lived computations. This disciplined scope usage leads to cleaner, more predictable behavior and easier debugging when values don’t change as you expect.

keyIdea.title: Scope guide
keyIdea.text: Use member variables for shared, persistent state; use local variables for temporary, function-scoped values to avoid unwanted side effects.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Variable Scope
Member Variables
Accessible anywhere in the Blueprint and persist with the actor.
When to use
Shared state like bIsOpen, PlayerHealth, or references to other actors.
Persistence
Remains until the actor is destroyed or the value is changed by Set nodes.
Local Variables
Scoped to a single function; used for temporary calculations.
When to use
Intermediate values inside a function that do not need to persist between events.
Common mistake
Trying to access a local variable outside its function. The Editor enforces scope and will not expose it.
Key Takeaway

Design variables with scope in mind: prefer member variables for shared state and locals for transient computations.

screens.title: Using Get and Set Nodes
screens.subtitle: Read and update variables in the Event Graph

narration.text: To interact with a variable in the Event Graph, drag its name from the My Blueprint panel into the graph. Choose Get to read the current value or Set to update it. A Get node outputs the variable’s current value and can feed into operations, comparisons, or function inputs. A Set node has an execution pin, so some event or sequence must trigger it; it also accepts an input value to write into the variable. For example, to increase PlayerScore when an enemy dies, Get PlayerScore, add the reward value with an Add node, then Set PlayerScore with the result hooked to the execution flow from the enemy-death event. Remember type matching: the Set node’s input expects the same type as the variable. If you try to plug a Float into an Integer input the Editor will warn or disallow the connection. Use conversion nodes only when appropriate. Also, after creating a variable, compile the Blueprint so Get and Set appear cleanly in context menus. Practicing Get and Set wiring will make event-driven logic intuitive: events trigger sequences, those sequences read and compute using Get nodes, and then write results back with Set nodes to change the actor’s state.

keyIdea.title: Get vs Set
keyIdea.text: Get returns a variable's value; Set writes a new value and requires an execution path to run.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Get and Set Nodes
Get and Set — read and write
Get outputs the current value. Set requires execution and an input value.
Typical flow
Event → Get current value → Compute → Set new value (execution pin from event).
Type check
Ensure the value plugged into Set has the same type as the variable to avoid warnings or errors.
Concrete example
// Blueprint-like pseudocode
Event EnemyDies
  Get PlayerScore
  Add PlayerScore + 10 -> Result
  Set PlayerScore = Result
This sequence reads the current score, adds a reward, and writes the updated score back using the Set node triggered by the EnemyDies event.

screens.title: Example: Increase PlayerSpeed with Get and Set
screens.subtitle: A concrete wiring example using numeric addition

narration.text: Let’s walk through a concrete example that uses Get, an Add node, and Set to increase a Float variable. Suppose you have a Float variable PlayerSpeed that starts at 400.0. When the player picks up a speed power-up you want to add 5.0 to PlayerSpeed. In the Event Graph drag PlayerSpeed and choose Get PlayerSpeed. From its output pin, add a Float + Float node and enter 5.0 in the second input. Drag PlayerSpeed again and choose Set PlayerSpeed. Connect the execution pin from the power-up Pickup event to the Set node’s execution input, and connect the Add output to the Set value. This sequence reads the current speed, computes the new speed, and updates the variable when the event triggers. A useful debugging step is to print the updated value after setting it so you can verify the change while running the level. Also be careful to match types; both inputs to the Add node must be Floats. If PlayerSpeed were an Integer, you would either change the variable to Float or use integer math. This example reinforces the Get → Compute → Set pattern that appears throughout Blueprint scripting. Try this wiring in your own Blueprint to see live updates when the pickup occurs.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Get the current value, compute the new value, then Set the variable using the event execution flow.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Increase PlayerSpeed
Wiring steps
A precise sequence for a Float increment using Get and Set.
// Pseudocode blueprint steps
Event PowerUpPickup
  Get PlayerSpeed         // current Float
  Add PlayerSpeed + 5.0   // Float + Float
  Set PlayerSpeed = Result  // update variable (execution pin from event)
  Print String("Speed: " + ToString(Result))  // optional debug
This pattern reads the current value, computes a new value with the Add node, and writes it back using Set, triggered by the pickup event.
Checklist
  • Ensure PlayerSpeed is a Float if you need decimals.
  • Connect execution pin from the event to the Set node.
  • Optionally print the new value to confirm at runtime.
Key Takeaway

Follow Get → Compute → Set to change values predictably and verify with debug prints while testing.

screens.title: Build BP_InteractiveDoor — Step-by-step
screens.subtitle: Hands-on: create the door actor, add variables and components

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through creating BP_InteractiveDoor to practice variables and components. First, in the Content Browser create a new Blueprint Class and choose Actor; name it BP_InteractiveDoor. Open the Blueprint and add a Static Mesh component, then set its mesh to a simple cube or a door-like shape; this visual will represent the door. Add a Text Render component and set its text to show the locked state. In the My Blueprint panel add a Boolean variable named bIsOpen and set its default to False. Add a Float variable DoorOpenSpeed with default 2.0 and an Integer RequiredKeys with default 1. Compile and Save. Place an instance of BP_InteractiveDoor in the level. To make it interactive, drag bIsOpen into the Event Graph as a Get and Set pair attached to an Interact event: when the player interacts and RequiredKeys conditions are met, Set bIsOpen to True and start an animation using DoorOpenSpeed. Consider adding an Object Reference variable such as PlayerReference or TargetDoor if you need the door to check the player's inventory. This activity encapsulates the full workflow: create components, add typed variables, set defaults, compile, and wire Get/Set to events. Try it now and observe how changing defaults affects the placed instance immediately.

keyIdea.title: Lab steps
keyIdea.text: Create BP_InteractiveDoor, add components, add typed variables with defaults, compile, place in level and wire Get/Set to events.

screens.title: Compile & Type Mismatch — Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Why variables sometimes don’t appear or accept values

narration.text: Two common problems beginners face are forgetting to compile and type mismatches. When you create or change a variable the Editor needs a Compile so that Get and Set appear cleanly and context menus update; if a freshly added variable does not show up when you try to drag it into the graph, the first step is to click Compile and Save. The second common issue is a type mismatch: each variable expects a specific data type. If you try to set an Integer with a Float value, or plug a String where a Float is expected, the Editor will either warn or prevent the connection. Understand why it occurs: the variable's type defines what the Set node will accept. If you need decimal math, use Float. If you must convert types deliberately, use explicit conversion nodes where provided. A typical workflow for debugging: check the variable type in Details, ensure the value or node you are connecting matches that type, and compile. Use debug prints to confirm values at runtime. These small checks resolve most variable-related issues quickly and keep your Event Graph behavior predictable.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting

Common mistakes and fixes
Two quick checks will solve most problems.
1. Forgot to Compile
If the variable won’t appear in the graph, click Compile and Save so the Editor updates available nodes and menus.
2. Type mismatch
Ensure the value you connect matches the variable’s type. If you need decimals use Float instead of Integer.
Debug tip
Use Print String or on-screen debug messages after setting a variable to verify runtime values and trace where incorrect values may be coming from.

screens.title: Object References: Linking Blueprints
screens.subtitle: Use references to let Blueprints interact with specific actors

narration.text: Object Reference variables let one Blueprint hold a direct link to another Actor or Component instance. This is different from storing raw data; a reference gives you access to the target’s properties and functions. For example, in BP_InteractiveDoor a variable TargetDoor of type BP_Door_C lets another system call an Open function or change the door’s bIsOpen variable. References are powerful because they enable communication between actors without polling or global state. To use an Object Reference, set its type to the appropriate Blueprint class in the Details panel. You can assign instances in the level through the Defaults or set them at runtime using Set. Be mindful of ownership and lifecycle: if the referenced actor is destroyed, the reference becomes invalid and you should guard access with validity checks. A common pattern is to expose an Object Reference as editable so level designers can assign targets in the editor, or to find and cache references at BeginPlay. This technique keeps systems decoupled yet connected, enabling modular interaction between actors in your level. What an Object Reference does
Stores a link to an Actor or Component instance so you can interact with that specific object.
Example

Assignment
Assign in the editor for level-placed references, or Set at runtime, for example during BeginPlay by finding actor instances.
Best practices
  • Expose references as editable when a designer should assign them in the level.
  • Cache references at BeginPlay if you need repeated access to avoid costly lookups.
  • Check validity before accessing a reference to avoid errors when the object is destroyed.
Key Takeaway

Use object references to connect actors for direct interaction, and guard access with validity checks if the target may be destroyed or nil.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. First, a variable is a named container that stores data for a Blueprint; choose the type that matches how you will use the data. Second, primitives include Boolean, Integer, Float, and String, while complex types include Vector, Rotator, Transform, and Object Reference for spatial or linked data. Third, scope matters: member variables persist on the actor and are accessible broadly, while local variables exist only inside a function. Fourth, use Get to read values and Set to write values, and remember that Set requires an execution path. Finally, always compile after creating or changing variables and watch for type mismatches. screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for everyday Blueprint work

narration.text: Keep three practical reminders at hand. First, always pick the variable type that reflects intended use: Booleans for true/false, Integers for whole counts, Floats for decimals, Strings for text, and structured types for spatial or referenced data. Second, name variables clearly and set sensible defaults so testing is immediate and your graphs are readable. Third, adopt the Get → Compute → Set pattern and compile frequently; these habits reduce errors, speed debugging, and make your Blueprints reliable.
